4.2.1||Tailwind: Experimenting with AI.quote: Okay, fantastic! You know, so one of the things he’s talked about is this model of, you know, the, the laboratory and the factory. You know, that inside your business and your MarTech stack, you kinda need to have both. You need to have the factory where, you know, the trains are running on time, and you’re, you’re very careful, uh, about the operations, but you also need the laboratory, where you’re in a position to experiment and try things and have things fail and break. But, you know, if you, if you try and… If, if you don’t separate those two environments, then you get either too conservative with the factory because you’re, like, just scared of breaking something, which is not a, a, a incorrect instinct, you know. Um, or yeah, if you’re just like, “Oh, well, we just gotta start trying all this stuff,” and you’re doing it in your actual, you know, production environment, yeah, you, you can break things. And so you need to have those sort of two different environments, and then only once you’ve found things in the laboratory that, you know, you now understand, you’ve proven like, okay, this is the dynamic, this is the guardrail, this is how it works, you know, then you can transfer that over into the factory. Um, but I think you definitely want to be pretty explicit, uh, about those two different models. Uh, and then the third thing would be what you were even framing in the question itself, which is focus on use cases. You know, ultimately, it comes down to like, okay, what is the specific thing we are looking to change? Whether it’s for how our business operates, or it’s the experience we’re delivering a customer, and how do we measure that? 4.2.1||Tailwind: Educating / Training /.name: Andreea Bulisache
4.2.1||Tailwind: Educating / Training /.quote: Notes on how she uses scenario planning to get boards to understand systems and implications So I would typically get involved in understanding how do you– what do you think is the, the way to go about AI? And my engagement typically starts with an AI governance war room. So I have a pre-designed sessions that exposes them to different scenarios in which they’re confronted with the, with the way they take decisions that are related to technology. And in my case, that would be exposure on the geopolitical front. So if you understand what your overdependency on a supplier that produces chipsets in, in Korea, and then once their op is open, then your whole business is exposed to it. Or, um, increased electricity costs, or how well do you understand, um, um, if it’s actually… So it’s for sure faster if you compare a human with a machine on the, on the ability to compute, but in some cases it’s cheaper to work with a human that has the whole context in his head, and he pays a set salary a month, versus paying all the, all the additional, um, uh, costs that are capacity, electricity, and beyond. So I do a lot of these scenario, scenario, uh, planning that would fit into articulating, uh, what does good look like? And not good look like, what does good look like from an AI standpoint? What does a good look like from a company overall perspective? And then how– what’s the, the perceived impact in the eyes of their customers and their stakeholders? And I think this might be a transferable thing to marketing. You could say, “Hey, what is– how will my client appreciate good for this particular product?”. “And then where can AI help me understand and operate this better?” And there’s a component of market research that is more of creative and, and stuff, so trends and whatever falls into- So that’s how I, I typically do it, and that’s an element of marketing reports, governance principles. There are different building blocks that span from, um, education, um, standards adoration, so companies need to be compliant with different evolving standards. Um, yeah. So that’s in a way- [Me] So then after such a session, I think you see that companies have, uh, a better understanding of what, what they want to do. They might have a more advanced thinking because they went through all those scenarios. Um, [lip smack] do, do you see that that is enough? Is that, that the core of where you help them, or is that the first step in the process? [Them] That’s the, that’s the– [chuckles] If anything, that’s the core of how I scare them. [Me] [laughing] [Them] So they, they think, they think they will have– they would, they would be up for a, an innovation session where with this AI expert that will inspire them on how the world will look like. And there I go, helping them understand how, how short-sighted they are with many things. So that continues to evolve with a series of additional sessions with multiple parties in the company. They will start knowing how to– what to ask of IT, and I work with their department, technology departments, to help articulate their, uh, their particular tech stack, work with consulting firms. Um, I help them, uh, design their criteria for vendor procurement, so what to ask from their particular vendors. Um, so there, it’s, it’s not the– it’s not a, it’s not an end game

4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.name: Lauren Stokowski

4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.name: Lauren Stokowski

4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.name: Sylvia Vroklage
4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.quote: The other side I think, there are also more established organizations that start with governance and completely lock things down before people are even allowed to get started. 4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.name: Tim Wiegel
4.2.4||Obstacle: high bureaucracy.quote: And I think a big problem you see, especially when I look at these enterprises, is that, uh, [Them] they are not allowed to use agentic AI a lot.
